title: Four basic tissue types and cell anatomy: illustrated foundations
description: Explore cell components and epithelial, connective, skeletal-muscle and nervous examples through four separate microscopic-scale teaching cutaways.

questions.question: What are the four basic types of tissue?
questions.answer: The broad categories are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Most organs contain multiple types; the images show specific teaching examples, not all subtypes.

questions.question: What makes epithelial tissue different from connective tissue?
questions.answer: Epithelia form close-packed sheets with apical and basal surfaces and little extracellular space. Connective-tissue cells are often dispersed in extracellular matrix. Epithelium is generally avascular and nourished from underlying tissues.

questions.question: Are these four pictures actual microscope slides?
questions.answer: No. They are digitally generated microscopic-scale educational cutaways rather than histology specimens, patient images, measured magnifications or diagnostic evidence.

questions.question: Which muscle type is shown in the foundation plate?
questions.answer: The striated, multinucleated parallel fibers depict a skeletal-muscle example. Smooth muscle is not striated, and cardiac muscle differs in branching and intercalated discs; neither has a dedicated picture in this batch.

questions.question: What structures make up nervous tissue?
questions.answer: Nervous tissue contains signaling neurons and supporting glial cells. The example shows a multipolar neuron with dendrites, an axon and myelin on some axon segments, not a map of a named clinical nerve.
